essays.stem: Describe the main types of housekeeping supplies, and explain how each type is used and stored.
essays.modelAnswer: Guest amenities are the items put in rooms for guests, such as soap, shampoo, lotion, shower caps, tissues, toilet rolls, stationery, and tea and coffee. They are stored clean and dry, on shelves off the floor, in date order so the oldest is used first. Cleaning agents are the chemicals used to clean, such as all-purpose cleaner, bowl cleaner, glass cleaner, disinfectant and polish. They are kept in their labelled containers, on low shelves, apart from food, amenities and linen, in a ventilated, locked area, with the safety data sheets close by. Cleaning equipment and small items include cloths, mops, buckets, brushes, gloves and vacuum bags; these are cleaned, dried and stored tidily after use so they do not grow germs. Linen, such as sheets and towels, is kept in the linen room or floor closet on clean shelves, away from chemicals.
markingPoints: Guest amenities named, with correct storage (dry, off the floor, in date order)
Cleaning chemicals named, with safe storage (labelled, low, apart, locked, SDS)
Equipment and small items, cleaned and dried before storage
Linen stored clean and away from chemicals
Explains how each type is used

essays.stem: Explain how par, minimum and maximum levels help housekeeping keep the right amount of supplies. Give a worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: A par level is the set amount of an item that should be in a pantry or on a trolley at the start of each day. The minimum level is the lowest safe amount; below it, the floor or store may run out before new stock arrives. The maximum level is the most that should be held, so money is not tied up and items do not expire or take up too much space. The reorder level sits between them: when stock falls to it, more is ordered. For example, a floor uses about 40 bars of soap a day and keeps 3 days' supply, so its par is 3 × 40 = 120 bars. At the end of the day the attendant counts 50 bars, so she requisitions 120 − 50 = 70 bars to bring the pantry back to par. Using these levels means guests always get what they need without waste.
markingPoints: Par level explained
Minimum level explained
Maximum level explained
Reorder level, or when to order, explained
Correct worked example of topping up to par

essays.stem: Describe how a room attendant's trolley should be stocked, kept and checked during a shift.
essays.modelAnswer: The trolley is stocked from the floor pantry using the standard list, so it has enough clean linen, amenities, toilet rolls and cleaning supplies for the rooms on her list. Heavy items, such as linen, go on the lower shelves so the trolley is stable, and clean linen is kept separate from the bag for soiled linen and the rubbish bag. Chemicals are in labelled bottles, closed, in a caddy that can be carried into the room and kept out of children's reach. While she cleans, the trolley is parked against the wall by the open door so it does not block the corridor. She keeps it tidy, does not let guests help themselves to large amounts, and records any extra items given to guests. At the end of the shift she empties the rubbish and soiled linen, wipes the trolley down, counts what is left, and tells the supervisor or requisitions what is needed.
markingPoints: Stocked from the pantry using the standard list
Heavy items low; clean and soiled kept apart
Chemicals labelled, closed and out of reach of guests and children
Parked safely by the door; extra issues recorded
Cleaned, counted and restocked at the end of the shift

essays.stem: Explain, step by step, how you would requisition supplies from the main store and record them on your floor.
essays.modelAnswer: First I count what is in the floor pantry and compare it with the par list, to work out how much of each item is needed. I fill in a requisition form with the date, my floor or section, each item, the amount needed and the unit (for example bottles, rolls or cases). I sign it and get my supervisor to sign or approve it, as the property's rules say. I take it to the store at the set time. When the storekeeper issues the goods, I check that the items and amounts match the form, and that nothing is damaged or out of date, before I sign for them. I take them to the pantry using a trolley, put the new stock behind the old stock, and store chemicals apart. Finally I update the floor stock record or bin card and keep my copy of the requisition.
markingPoints: Counts pantry stock and compares with par
Completes the requisition form fully (date, items, amounts)
Gets it signed or approved and takes it to the store
Checks goods against the form before signing for them
Stores new stock behind old and updates the records

essays.stem: Explain how to store and handle housekeeping chemicals safely, including dilution, labelling, and what to do after a spill or a splash to the eye.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the label and the safety data sheet before using a chemical. Chemicals are kept in their original or properly labelled containers, closed, on low shelves in a ventilated, locked area, away from food, amenities and linen. I never put them in drink bottles and never mix products, especially bleach with ammonia or acid cleaners, because toxic gas can form. I wear gloves, and eye protection when pouring concentrates. I dilute using the dispenser or a measure, as the maker's label says, adding chemical to water, and label every spray bottle with the product name and dilution. If there is a spill I put out a wet-floor sign, keep people away, and clean it up wearing PPE as the SDS says, then report it. If a chemical splashes into someone's eye, I rinse the eye with plenty of clean running water, get first-aid help and take the SDS or label to the doctor.
markingPoints: Reads the label and SDS; stores labelled, closed, low, locked and apart
Never uses drink bottles and never mixes products (bleach and ammonia)
Wears PPE and dilutes as the label says, labelling spray bottles
Spill: wet-floor sign, PPE, clean up as the SDS says, report
Eye splash: rinse with plenty of running water, first aid, take the label or SDS

essays.stem: Explain how housekeeping can control the cost of supplies and reduce waste.
essays.modelAnswer: Housekeeping controls cost first by setting par levels, so there is enough stock but not too much. Issues from the store are made only on signed requisitions, and pantries are locked and counted, so losses show up quickly. Supervisors compare the supplies used with the number of rooms cleaned; if use jumps, they look for waste or theft. Attendants follow the room standard list instead of putting extra items in rooms. Chemicals are diluted with measured dispensers, which saves product and keeps the strength right. Stock is rotated so nothing expires, and damaged items are recorded and reported. Bulk shower dispensers, towel reuse programmes and recycling cut waste. Buying in bulk where storage allows can lower the cost of each item. Finally, staff are trained to care for equipment, such as cleaning and drying mops and cloths, so it lasts longer.
markingPoints: Par levels and controlled, signed issues
Locked storage and regular counts to spot loss
Follows room standards; measured chemical dilution
Stock rotation and recording damage to reduce waste
Refill dispensers, towel reuse, recycling, bulk buying or equipment care

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a count of the supplies in a floor pantry, and what you would do about any difference from the records.
essays.modelAnswer: I would agree a time with my supervisor when no items are being issued, so the count is accurate. I would take the stock sheet that lists every item and its unit. I would count each shelf in order, item by item, including open boxes and items on trolleys, and write the amounts clearly in pen. A colleague can count again to check. I would note any items that are damaged or out of date separately. Then I would compare each count with the balance on the stock record. If there is a difference, I would recount that item first. If the difference is still there, I would check the requisitions and issue sheets for missing entries. Any difference I cannot explain I would report to the supervisor in writing, with the item, the amount and the date, and not change the records myself.
markingPoints: Plans the count at a quiet time with the stock sheet
Counts every item in order, including trolleys, and records clearly
Notes damaged or expired items separately
Compares with records and recounts any difference
Checks the paperwork and reports unexplained differences in writing

essays.stem: Explain how housekeeping supplies can be kept secure from theft and loss.
essays.modelAnswer: Pantries, linen closets and stores are kept locked when no one is working in them. Keys are given only to named staff, signed out and signed back in on a key log, and never left in doors or taken home. Supplies are issued only against signed requisitions, and issue sheets record what each attendant takes. Trolleys are parked by the room door, not left unattended in public areas, so guests and visitors cannot help themselves. Regular stock counts compare the stock with the records, and supervisors watch how much is used per room cleaned. Any shortage is reported at once. Bags may be checked as the property's policy says, staff are trained in the rules, and good, honest work is encouraged. Damaged and expired items are recorded, not just thrown away, so the records stay true.
markingPoints: Pantries and stores locked
Keys controlled with a key log
Issues only on signed requisitions and issue sheets
Trolleys not left unattended; extra issues recorded
Regular counts, usage checks and reporting of shortages

essays.stem: Explain how a property's occupancy and events affect the supplies housekeeping needs. Use a Jamaican example.
essays.modelAnswer: The more rooms that are occupied, the more amenities, toilet rolls, linen and chemicals are used, because every occupied room is cleaned and restocked each day. The supervisor checks the occupancy forecast each week and plans stock to match. For example, a hotel in Montego Bay is usually much busier in the winter tourist season, from about December to April, than in the slow months. Before the season it raises par levels and orders early, so it does not run out when suppliers are busy. Events also matter: a wedding, a conference or a group of cruise visitors can mean extra guest rooms, more toilets to service in public areas, and extra cleaning after functions. Departures need more supplies than stay-over rooms. Before a hurricane warning the property may also need extra stock of basic items in case deliveries stop. Good planning means guests always find what they need.
markingPoints: More occupied rooms means more supplies used
Uses the occupancy forecast to plan stock
Jamaican example: busy tourist season, raise par and order early
Events or groups increase needs (public areas, functions)
Other factors such as departures or storm preparation

essays.stem: Describe how you would check, report and deal with damaged, faulty or expired supplies and equipment.
essays.modelAnswer: I check supplies when I receive them from the store, when I stock my trolley and during counts. I look for broken or leaking bottles, torn packs, products that look or smell wrong, and dates that have passed. I check equipment such as vacuum cleaners for split cords, damaged plugs, full bags and strange noises before I use it. If a supply is damaged or expired, I take it out of use at once, keep it apart and labelled, and record it on the damaged-stock sheet. If a product is faulty, such as toilet rolls that tear easily, I keep a sample and tell my supervisor so the supplier can be told. Faulty equipment is switched off, unplugged, tagged "do not use" and reported for repair. Leaking chemicals are handled with gloves and cleaned up as the SDS says. I never hide damage, because the records must stay correct.
markingPoints: Checks supplies and equipment at receipt, trolley stocking and counts
Removes damaged or expired items and keeps them apart and labelled
Records them on the damaged-stock sheet and reports
Faulty equipment unplugged, tagged and reported
Keeps a sample of faulty products; leaks handled safely as the SDS says

practical1.title: Stock room attendant trolleys and a floor pantry to par
practical1.brief: The assessor sets up the Centre's housekeeping room (or a mock floor pantry) with a par list, a mixed and partly used stock of amenities, toilet rolls, linen and cleaning products, some items out of date or damaged, and two or three room attendant trolleys. As a group: count the pantry and compare it with the par list; complete a requisition for what is short; set aside, label and record any damaged or expired items; and stock each trolley to the standard list, with heavy items low, clean and soiled kept apart and chemicals in a closed caddy. Each member stocks one trolley or section and fills one spray bottle, diluting the Centre's approved cleaner as its label says (or using water if the assessor says), and labels it with the product name and dilution. Then clean and tidy the pantry and record the closing stock. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and forms to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Par list and standard trolley list (from the assessor)
Guest amenities, toilet rolls, tissues and linen (real or mock)
Cleaning products with labels and safety data sheets
Spray bottles, measuring jug and labels
Room attendant trolleys with caddies and soiled-linen bags
Requisition forms, stock sheets and damaged-stock sheet
photos: The completed count sheet and requisition
The damaged and expired items set apart and labelled
Each stocked trolley, showing heavy items low and chemicals in the caddy
The tidy pantry and the closing stock record
checklist: Counted their section accurately and compared it with par
Worked out the amounts to requisition correctly
Found, set apart and recorded damaged or expired items
Stocked a trolley to the standard list, safely loaded
Diluted and labelled a chemical correctly, wearing PPE
Stored chemicals apart from amenities and linen
Left the pantry clean and the records complete
safety: Read the label and SDS before handling any chemical; never mix products
Wear gloves, and eye protection when pouring concentrate
Lift heavy boxes with bent knees, or use a trolley or a partner
Keep walkways clear and put out a wet-floor sign for any spill

practical2.title: Plan housekeeping supplies for a busy week from an occupancy forecast
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group an occupancy forecast for a 30-room villa property or small hotel for one busy week in the tourist season, a room standard list (the amenities and supplies each occupied room gets each day), and the current stock in the housekeeping store. As a group: (1) work out how much of each item will be used each day and over the week; (2) set a par, a minimum and a maximum for at least six items; (3) compare with the stock on hand and prepare a requisition or order list, with the units; (4) make a stock card for two items and record a week of issues and receipts; and (5) present a short poster on ways to cut waste and loss of supplies. Each member takes the lead on one part and checks another member's sums. Every member must explain one figure to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and sheets to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Occupancy forecast, room standard list and stock figures (from the assessor)
Stock sheets, stock cards and requisition or order forms
photos: The usage working for each day and the week
The table of par, minimum and maximum levels
The completed requisition or order list
The stock cards with a week of entries
The poster on cutting waste and loss
A member explaining a figure to the assessor
checklist: Worked out daily and weekly use correctly from the forecast
Set sensible par, minimum and maximum levels
Prepared a clear requisition or order list with units
Checked another member's sums and corrected mistakes
Explained a figure clearly to the assessor
Gave practical ideas to cut waste and loss
safety: Keep the property's stock and cost figures confidential
Sit comfortably and take short breaks
Keep bags and cables out of walkways
Treat team members with respect when checking their work
